analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear argument next to number 871206, Catherine Isabella Mesa versus California. Excuse me, sir. Thank you. The question that's presented here is whether such a prosecution is one, quote, for acts under color of office and is therefore removable under 28 U.S.C. section 1442A1. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, in this case, responded to that question in the negative. And the respondent here supports the reasoning adopted by that court, which reasoning is essentially that one is only acting under color of office in the context of this statute, where one is raising a federal law defense to the charge that is brought. So, the United States and the petitioners in this case believe that this is a narrow and a grudging interpretation of the statute. And we take that position essentially because it's an interpretation that will clearly fail to accomplish the clear purposes of the statute. Mr. Ayer, is Section 1442A1 a jurisdictional statute? Or does it independently support arising under jurisdiction in the courts? It is a statute. It is a statute conferring jurisdiction on the federal courts in matters which do arise under the Constitution and laws of the United States. Well, it seemed to me that perhaps the statute doesn't independently support arising under jurisdiction and that to adopt the view that you do might present some Article III jurisdiction problems. Without a federal defense, what is the arising under jurisdiction? Well, we believe that there's a number of answers to that question, and it's a very long answer if one is to give it in any sort of a complete way. It's an answer that has been much debated over a long period of years and which this court, I think, has addressed only peripherally in its decisions. I would start by saying that this case arises under federal law in the sense that, first, it arises on account of federal law, that is, on account of the federal laws creating the United States Postal Service and giving it certain responsibilities. This case would never have come to court had the Postal Service not been created and various individuals employed by it put in motion in a certain way to accomplish a certain function. Secondly, it arises under in the sense that it is a challenge that the prosecution in California is a challenge to the conduct of a federal official in the performance of his official duties. That isn't to say that it will ultimately be decided necessarily that his conduct was justified and is not subject to criminal prosecution. That's the issue that has to be decided in the action once removed. But it is a challenge to the way the job was done. It says arising under federal law, not arising because of the existence of the federal government or arising in the performance of some federal acts. It's arising under federal law. We've always thought that meant that federal law had to have something to do with deciding the case, and that would seem to be the reason you would want to put that in federal courts. Well, I think there are two parts of the answer I'd like to give to that. The first is that there has been a theory which has been much discussed, the theory of protective jurisdiction. And it is arguable, I'm not conceding that it's true, but it's arguable that in order to find jurisdiction arising under here, one must adopt some variation of that theory. What I would suggest is that if one must do that, it is a very narrow and easily confinable form of that theory, that it is protective jurisdiction to protect the activities of the federal government itself. Secondly... Inherent. Inherent. And without any authorization from Congress. Well, the authorization in Congress comes in the statute... Arising under federal law. In the statute, the removal statute here. In other words, it's a conferral of jurisdiction to decide issues that are of federal interest where, let us assume for the moment, there is no federal law actually operative. I think it's a stretching thing to say that Congress intended that states have to prosecute traffic offenses in federal courts, which could be, in fact, miles from the scene of the accidents. It's a very strained interpretation. Well, Justice O'Connor, I think what one must do to decide how strained it is is focus on the operative effect of the interpretation, on the one hand, that we offer and, on the other hand, that the respondent offers in this case and the Court of Appeals adopted. Number one, I think, if one starts with the historical situation that gave rise to these statutes, you are talking, starting in 1815, with the embargo in the War of 1812 and the resistance on the part of local governments, the nullification crisis around 1830, and the 1833 statute to deal with specific state resistance to that. Well, I think if you look at the history and apply it, it certainly wasn't enacted just to protect the presence of a federal employee. It was to deal with a conflicting federal law. Well, I think, Your Honor, I would disagree slightly and suggest that what it was intended to do was to deal with a perceived problem of bias, hostility, and interference, which doesn't come up all the time, but which can come up and historically, demonstrably had come up. And I'd like to give a hypothetical case to illustrate what I'm talking about. If you assume the situation of a federal criminal investigation that is ongoing in some locality and is generally known to be ongoing, and let's say an FBI agent is, in the course of that investigation, involved or at least present at the scene of a shootout that occurs, two situations. One, he is accused, let's say, of murder, of someone who ends up dying in the course of that shootout. And, in fact, the evidence is clear that he did shoot the person. And his response is, yes, I shot him, but I did this in the course of performing my federal duty. There you have a federal defense. There you have removal. Let's suppose, however, that instead of saying that, and, in fact, the facts support his view and his conclusion, that he did not shoot the person. And, indeed, what has happened is, let's say, to make it as extreme as possible, he has indeed been framed or that there is some indication that he may have been framed. And his answer is not that I did this in the course of performing my federal duty. His answer is I didn't do it. I wasn't there or whatever defense can be offered. I would submit that in that circumstance, given the distinction that has been rested on here by the Ninth Circuit, that case can't be removed. And it is at least as urgent a situation calling for removal. Why should that case be removed? Why should that case be removed? Why can't the state courts give him a fair trial on whether he shot the man? Well, now I think, Justice Stevens, we're talking about the premise of the statute. The premise of the statute is, and one can disagree with it, but the premise of the statute is that there is a problem of state interference, sometimes a problem of state interference, state hostility, state bias, and that that justifies the removal of cases to federal court. Should not the party wanting removal make such an allegation? Well, the problem, the whole problem that's involved in removal, I think, Your Honor, is that one cannot know at the time of removal, number one, either whether the person is a good guy or a bad guy, whether he did something that was proper or he did something that was improper, nor can one know in every instance whether there is bias, hostility, or harassment or something like that. Now, there are extreme cases. Well, what kind of a presumption should we adopt? You know, thousands of state courts out there, they're all biased? We do not think that one needs to guess very much about the rule, because we think that the language of the statute is reasonably clear. When one talks in terms of action under color of office, it is not an absolutely precise term, but it's a term that generally has the meaning of with the appearance of or in apparent performance of office. And we think that that is a perfectly reasonable reading to apply in this situation. May I ask just two questions? Does it apply equally in a civil case, a civil toward action? Say somebody is a fender bender with a postal worker as a defendant. Well, we think that the basic standard, the basic question that must be asked, which we would submit, is is this a case where it appears at the time of removal that the federal official was acting in the performance of his duty? He was. He was driving the mail truck. And he hopped into somebody. That that same standard should apply in both a civil and a criminal case. Now, so every tort case involving a federal employee who is engaged in his regular work can be removed to federal court. Well, Your Honor, I would submit that from this court's decision in Willingham, that much with regard to the federal case is quite clear because in Willingham, the court indicated that all one needed to show was a causal connection between the prosecution and the performance of one's job. Now, there's a footnote in Willingham that my opponent will, I'm sure, bring up, and so I'll bring it up first, which indicates that I think the words are essentially a more specific showing may be required in a criminal case. So the argument may be that it's easier to remove a case where it's civil than where it's criminal. And my point would be that the more specific showing may well involve a requirement of more detail on the part of the government. If there's any doubt about whether he was actually performing his job, if he was in the course of performing his job, then he may have a heavier burden of showing that, a more detailed showing of that. But I would submit... Showing that he was really at work? Showing that what... Well, you have to, I think, look at two cases. One is where he, in fact, did the act, which I think we can take this case as an example of, where there were accidents involved, and he was driving his postal route. These are alleged negligent violations. Most motor vehicle accidents, it's not hard to prove who was driving. I mean, you know, you start there. Then the question is, in your position, in all traffic accident cases, in which somebody wants to sue a federal employee who was at work at the time, they can all be... The jurisdiction should have all those cases in the federal court. Well, I think that's right. Now, the different case, obviously, would be where a postal driver is off on a lark and a detour and... I understand, but you've got a lot of cases where they're not on larks and detours. They're just driving the regular mail route. That's right. And that, I think... The causal connection that we referred to in Willingham was simply that he happened to be at work at the time. He had to be in the course of performing his job. Why not... He wouldn't have been alive because if he didn't have this federal job, he wouldn't have had food and he would have died. Is that a causal connection? It's the only job he had. I don't think that's the kind of causal connection that the court has. Ah, so we have to decide some kind of causal connection. It isn't clear that it's a causal connection. Well, but I think if you look at the fact... You think it's enough just that he was at work rather than it was necessary that he do this thing in the course of his work. The specific thing alleged to have been negligent was something that's much more approximately related to the directions of his... I think it is definitely, as you state, Justice Scalia, and the reason is in part to be found in this court's... Well, that's not just driving a car. I mean, any time you're driving a car anywhere during your work hours, that's enough of a causal connection. I'm suggesting that may not be enough. Well, when someone's job is to be a postal delivery person and one is driving one's mail truck and one is going from pickup point A to pickup point B and doing it by the shortest route or by the usual route, it seems to me that it clearly is a situation where he is in the course of performing his job, and that should be enough. There is... How do these cases unfold? The state tries to prosecute someone for an ordinary traffic accident, as here, and it turns out it's a federal postal worker. Now, does the U.S. attorney intervene and represent that person just because they're an employee? The...there's a decision to be made with regard to representation, which decision is based upon... a decision, I think, by the United States attorney as to, number one, whether he believes the action was in the scope of employment, and, number two, whether representation and removal is in the interest of the United States. Is this a case where the U.S. attorney got the idea of removal and removed it, or was this something the employees did on their own? Well, the employees were represented by the United States attorney's office and by an attorney in the United States attorney's office. I would hasten to add, however, and I can...based in part on personal experience, that it is not uniformly and always the case that these cases are removed to federal court, I myself having represented a postal carrier and done it in state court. It is a decision that must be made, and the idea... How many of these do we get, Mr. A? Well, I think it's interesting. I think the allegation that... I can't give you statistics, but the allegation that if the court decides the case the way we urge, there is going to be some deluge of cases that is going to bury the federal courts, there's several things wrong with that. One is that the United States attorneys and the United States government has been operating, rightly or wrongly, and you will let us know that, under the theory that the rule is as we maintain, that the decisions to remove have been made on this basis. And there is no flood of these cases. Anyone who has worked in a United States attorney's office or in a district attorney's office cannot cite to you, you know, ten dozen of these cases that have come along. They simply don't come along in that office. I suppose the private counsel for the employee has the option to remove, whether the United States attorney wants to or not. That's certainly right. He certainly would have. But if you've got a parking ticket, that gets removed to federal court if it's a… If it involves an act under color of office in the performance of the job. It can. And I want to stress, it's a decision that must be made in each case, whether it makes sense. Does Congress constitutionally have the authority to pass a statute which says any federal employee, it's a privilege of his employment, can remove any case to the federal court? I don't know. I, I, I, any case involving, say… Any time, any time a federal employee sued, just as a… Well, I think… As an incident to your employment, you have the right to go to federal court. You would have a more difficult time demonstrating arising under jurisdiction. I'm not saying that it couldn't conceivably be done, but it would certainly be more difficult than this case, where we are talking about conduct in the performance of official federal functions and disputes about how those functions… Well, what's the federal law that would appear in that case, and what's the federal law that appears in this case? Well… Okay, let me, let me go back to the, to the question of the arising under jurisdiction and, and what federal law is present. My, my first point is that it is not clear, given the protective jurisdiction theory, and I, I would hasten to point out that there are a number of, first of all, cases of this court, starting with the Osborne and the Bank of the United States case, but proceeding to other cases involving federally chartered corporations, the Pacific Railroad removal cases in, I think, 159 U.S., in the, in, in the matter of Dunn in 212 U.S. These are cases brought against federally chartered corporations, not brought by, but brought against federally chartered corporations, where the court found jurisdiction simply based on the fact that you had a federally chartered corporation. Now, subsequently, in 28 U.S.C. 1349, Congress has enacted a law that says there is only jurisdiction in that circumstance where the capital stock is owned more than half by the government of the United States. So it has recognized jurisdiction, Congress has jurisdiction predicated on this theory. So the first point, I guess I would, and one other thing, there are, there are several federal statutes now on the books, now operative, now being enforced every day, including those concerning the FDIC. I think it's 28 U.S.C., no, 12 U.S.C., 1819, and one called the Edge Act involving jurisdiction over matters involving banks, international disputes involving banks. I think that's 12 U.S.C. 632. The Bankruptcy Act, slightly different because there's constitutional basis, but trustees in bankruptcy can, as a matter of federal court jurisdiction, pursue state law disputes in connection with the bankruptcies. Well, what's the policy that you're trying to further in this case, this class of cases? What is the federal interest that we have? You mean these cases? Yes. Well, these are cases where, if one looks at the papers in the record, in the excerpt of Record on Appeal in particular, one can see that they are, they have certain peculiarities. I am not suggesting that there is the bias or the harassment or whatever else, because I don't know. And one can't know at this stage of a case, I think, typically. But these are cases, on the one hand, where, in the Mesa case, we have a collision and resulted in a fatality of a young bicycle rider who was riding on the wrong side of the road and ran into, head on, the front of this mail truck. Now, I am not saying, I'm not suggesting that I'm concluding where fault lies, but that is itself a somewhat unusual situation. But you're suggesting that would be an occasion for bias? Well, I'm suggesting that when the matter was presented, presented for decision by the attorney handling the case as to what to do with it, one of the things that he could reasonably consider, in fact, really about the only thing he knew about the case at that time, was a question of what are the merits, what do the merits appear to be, what do the facts appear to be of this case? There appeared to be an issue in this case with regard to the merits of the violation, and whether or not there is a question of bias is something that you can't know at that point. Well, but why would he look at this as anything other than a garden-variety traffic accident case? Well, he would look to see... I mean, Bill, why would he view in this case anything as special that might suggest bias against the federal government or against a federal government employee? Let me give you the other case, which may or may not partially answer your question. The other case is one that involves allegations of speeding and another offense where what actually happened was a police car struck the rear, I think right, I'm not sure right or left, but the rear side of the mail truck, and the allegation was that the mail truck was speeding. One wonders, in that circumstance, at least I would, knowing those facts, one wonders why the case was brought in the context of that kind of a set of facts. And one can't know, and I can't even suggest that there necessarily is any impropriety or bias or uncertainty, but the fact that there's the possibility of that... Why is there the possibility on those facts? I mean, other than you might say, I suppose, that bias might play a part in any case. But why on those facts is there any reason to think it's any different than any other case? There is reason... There is not reason to believe. There is reason to wonder. And the reason is that, as I've described it, I think those facts are susceptible if you fill them in with other facts, which I don't have. But if you fill them in with other facts and circumstances, it is possible that there was a motivation for bringing the prosecution that was improper, whether it was... You're asking us to say that we erect a presumption that there is a real potential for bias in the state courts. Isn't that what you're asking us? Well, I don't think you have to erect any presumption. We believe that the statute has been written in a way that plainly allows a choice to be made, which... Let us assume that we must find some federal interest beyond the mere employment status. Is that interest the fact that there is a real potential for bias? Is that what you're asking us to say? I think what I'm asking you to say is that Congress has reasonably decided that there is always a reasonable potential for bias. And on that basis, the cases may be moved from state court to federal court. And the problem is that just as one cannot know whether the defendant, the federal official, is in the right or in the wrong, you don't find that out until after the case is over, one cannot know whether one is going to get a fair trial in state court or not. I'm not saying that most of the time you're not. I'm sure that's not true. I'm sure most of the time you are going to get a fair trial. But Congress has said that where you have essentially a federal function being challenged in state court, we care enough about that that we want that in the federal court. Yes, but, Mr. Aaron, the example you put, the possibility of bias because there are police officers involved, is what I suppose you're suggesting. They might have wanted to cover up their own negligence, and therefore they brought a charge. Well, he ran into a mail truck. All right, but that same bias would be potential if the defendant were a private citizen rather than a federal employee. That's bias in favor of something unrelated to the federal official. Well, and, you know, now you're... You're just suggesting that the federal officials ought to have some special defense that the ordinary citizen does not have. I'm not suggesting that they ought to. I'm suggesting that Congress has decided that they want challenges to federal functions to be in federal court if the judgment is made that that's, in the given case, what ought to happen. That's the way the statute is written. And I think that Congress had the authority to do that. And all we are doing in arguing this, I think, is trying to put the statute in a form that will accomplish the job. The problem is if you don't read it the way we read it, and you actually have a situation where there is very good reason to believe that a local community and a local government is completely hostile and is going to throw up every barrier it can, including staging accidents and framing federal officials and prosecuting them for one thing and another, you don't have a removal statute. Those were the kinds of problems that were being addressed in 1815 and in 1833, where states were openly hostile and where they were taking affirmative actions to stop the enforcement of federal law. In those cases, the statutes were tailor-made to particular situations and for limited periods of time. Well, they were not all for limited periods of time. There's a nationwide assumption that this goes on all over the country. At the time of Nagel, what year was Nagel? Was there a statute? Roughly 1890 or thereabouts. Was there a statute then? Yes. Not this one, though, was it? Well, it was in process of evolution. There was the 1866 statute which used the phrase under color of law. There's no question that the hostility was very evident toward the United States Marshal in the Nagel case. That's right. That's quite different from this. Well, that was a habeas corpus. I know. Not a removal. Bob took the people off the train. Oh, that's right. But the remedy is different. On the one hand, the remedy in habeas corpus is essentially to intervene and put a stop to the state prosecution. Here, we are bringing it into the federal forum. Your Honor, if I could, I'd like to save the remainder of my time for rebuttal. Very well, Mr. Error. Mr. Rosenblatt, we'll hear now from you. Thank you. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. This court has never allowed removal where a federal official has not had a federal defense. This court should not change its enforcement of the federal defense requirement for several reasons. First, there's clear legislative history indicating that Congress intended to require a federal defense. Second, this court in a long line of cases has accepted that legislative history and has applied it in favor of the federal defense requirement. Third, allowing removal without a federal defense would not only burden state and local governments, but would also burden federal courts for no discernible purpose. I'd like to discuss all of those reasons, but first I'd like to clear up a matter of fact. I've handled these cases since the beginning. At the district court, there was no allegation of harassment. At the Ninth Circuit, there was no allegation of harassment. If this court looks at the Ninth Circuit opinion at page 967, the court specifically states that the removal petitions at issue here contain no allegation of a pattern of enforcement. If there were an allegation of harassment, would that suffice? Yes, under certain circumstances. How do you draft the allegation of harassment so that you come within the statute as you understand the statute? I believe this court stated the exact procedure to follow in its case of SOPR number one. I read that as an harassment case primarily because of language that's also in SOPR number two. The way you do it is simple. You set out in your removal petitions everything that you did. You show that those acts were protected by federal law. You also must show some hint or some suggestion from the facts of the case that the prosecution was not legitimately motivated. Therefore, by the negative pregnant, it must have been motivated or commenced upon account of some act that you did that is protected by your federal authority. In a criminal case, that doesn't impinge on the defendant's Fifth Amendment rights? No. As a matter of fact, this court in SOPR one specifically stated that the Fifth Amendment privilege must be waived. I'm comfortable with that for several reasons. The first is that the waiver only goes towards stating a federal defense. It's more of a prosecutorial discovery that in any event would have been obtained. Second, the defendant is not stuck with that defense because an allegation that's made for removal does not bind the defendant at trial, as happened, in fact, in Arizona v. Menipan. Well, you began by saying he has to set forth everything that he did. That is correct, but we assume that he would do so in order to avail himself of the federal defense. I concede the point. However, this court, since Tennessee v. Davis, has made that clear that the Fifth Amendment privilege must be waived, and it's because it's such an exceptional procedure that we're talking about here. We're talking about taking a case out of the state courts, and in order to do that, the federal official must give some reason why federal jurisdiction, which is usually strictly construed, should be afforded to his case. And he has to tell us, essentially, that the prosecution challenges federal law. Otherwise, he is consigned to the state courts. Mr. Rosenblatt, you mentioned Tennessee v. Davis, and that's a case that the Solicitor General argues allowed removal based strictly on the federal employee's assertion of self-defense under state law. I would disagree. And it could be read that way, I guess. I don't believe, with all respect, it can be read that way. In my brief, I simply stated every sentence of Tennessee v. Davis is somewhat inconsistent, and I may just have to repeat that with particular reference to pages 261 and 262. Indeed, the court, in assessing the constitutionality of the statute, which is what it was doing in Tennessee v. Davis, said that it only went so far as to look at what happens when there is a federal defense. And the final lines of Tennessee v. Davis, I think, say it very well about what the court actually was doing. I might just take a moment. On page 272, when this is understood, and it is time it should be, it will not appear strange that, even in cases of criminal prosecutions for alleged offenses against the state, in which arises a defense under United States law, the general government should take cognizance of the case and try it in its own courts, according to its own forms of proceeding. I believe that a fair reading of Tennessee v. Davis mandates the idea, and that the federal defense requirement was what they were considering. Indeed, a fair reading of the mayor v. Cooper, I believe, leads us to the same point. Mr. Rosenblatt, how does the existence of harassment equate with the existence of a federal defense? It implicates the supremacy clause of the United States Constitution. That is how we get to a federal defense. Why? Do you have to be harassed because you're a federal employee, or do they just have something in for you? They don't like postmen. They wouldn't care whether postmen were federal employees or not, or they don't like some other thing about you that has nothing to do with your federal status. I'm a little unclear, Justice, because if they don't like you because you're a postman, that does implicate some hostility against federal authority. If they don't like you because of the color of your hair, you cannot get removal. You may, however... So you say there must be harassment specifically on a ground that is related to your federal activity. Absolutely, and that's what this court said in SOPR number one. So you would say there is no harassment possible where you are picking on a truck that you ran into. You're a policeman. You run into the truck, as has happened here. That is not harassment by reason of your federal character. That's correct. It may well be harassment, and there may be other means of availing yourself of a remedy, but as far as this statute is concerned for federal employees, it would not be enough to gain removal. And it raises a federal question when you're harassing someone because of his federal character. Why? Because you're attempting to interfere with his enforcement of federal law. That is, if you take a postman off the street, he isn't able to deliver the mail, and if you do so because you're hostile to the federal government... Why does that cause the action to arise under federal law? Because that... Once you depart from that language, you risk enabling me to agree with the government that, well, the language doesn't really mean arising under, and if it doesn't mean arising under, then I can think of a lot of different things it might mean. I assume we're talking about the Article III arising under here, and the reason that it would do so is that it would arise under the Supremacy Clause of the United States. That would be my position as to why this case would arise... The suit would arise under the... I think the harassment might implicate the Supremacy Clause, but I don't see how the lawsuit would arise under the Supremacy Clause. However, let me make a distinction. The well-pleaded complaint rule, which usually guides us in the 1331 situation, doesn't guide us here. So a defense that raises federal law is enough to make a case arise under Article III. That's how I believe the case would arise under Article III. Obviously, there have been some concerns stated about harassment, and I'd like to reassure the court that there is no way in which a ruling in our favor will impede a federal official in gaining a remedy if he is harassed. First, of course, the federal official may file for habeas corpus, the precise thing that happened in Inre Nagel. And as to my colleague's comment that he would not know if he was harassed until at some future date, first, you can file a greater habeas corpus any time before trial, and by trial you ought to know if you have been harassed. The same can be said for removal, of course. But habeas corpus before trial is certainly not a favored remedy in the federal court. It is for federal officials under this court's decisions in Ex-Rel Drury, and I cite those decisions in our brief. For federal officials, anticipatory habeas corpus is, I submit, a favored remedy.
